title: A high-pressure profession, by its nature
paras: Planning is a high-pressure profession by its nature. Every planner, sooner or later, has one of those weeks — three deadlines at once, a committee going against a careful recommendation, an unhappy client, an appeal you didn't see coming. That's where the difference shows: between the planners who last and the ones ground down by it. And it's rarely about talent — it's about how they cope. You can't make the pressure go away, but you can get much better at carrying it, and the habits that let you are simple and open to anyone.

The job is, and always will be, demanding — deadlines that don't move, like determination dates, committee cycles and appeal timetables; decisions that carry real consequences and often a lot of money; and a permanent place between competing interests, where pleasing one party disappoints another, all in public and on the record. Much unnecessary suffering comes from treating that as a problem to solve rather than a condition to manage. What changes over a career isn't the work but your relationship with it: the experienced planner isn't under less strain, they've just learned to hold it more lightly. So the first lesson is to stop expecting the pressure to disappear and get good at living with it.

One from my own experience — the email I did not send. I used to answer everything the instant it arrived, evenings and weekends, and was quietly proud of it. The habit broke the night I fired off a terse reply to a difficult client at ten o'clock, tired and irritated, and spent the next morning undoing the damage. Now anything that lands after I've stopped for the day waits until morning. Nothing was ever made worse by a night's sleep — and a great deal made better.

title: Pressure you can ride, and stress that grinds
paras: Now — there's pressure you can ride, and there's stress that grinds. Short bursts are normal, often useful: finishing a report for Thursday's committee, the focus a public inquiry demands, the adrenaline before a difficult meeting. They pass, and a career is full of them. Most planners rather enjoy this kind — it sharpens the mind, and there's satisfaction in rising to it and coming down again.

The other kind deserves your attention — pressure that never lets up, that grinding sense of being permanently behind month after month with no recovery in between. Learn to tell them apart. The warning signs: exhaustion a weekend no longer fixes, dread of the working day, enjoyment draining out of the job, sleep going wrong, a shorter temper, small mistakes creeping into work you'd normally get right. A hard fortnight isn't this; a hard six months with those signs settling in is a signal to take seriously and act on.

title: Keeping a sense of proportion
paras: If one mental habit protects a planner more than any other, it's a sense of proportion — and you need it most when it's hardest to find. A refusal at committee, a lost appeal, a scheme you championed thrown out. In the moment these feel like disasters, and the mind runs to the worst: that your judgement's failing, that the client will walk. That's catastrophising, and it's almost always a liar. The most useful question after a setback: will this matter in a year? Now and then, yes — and then you learn from it. Far more often, no.

Some of this comes with experience — the hundredth refusal doesn't wound like the first. But you can practise it deliberately. Resist drawing sweeping conclusions from a single event: a lost appeal is one inspector's view, on one scheme, on one day, not a verdict on your ability, and even excellent planners lose cases they should have won. Holding that proportion while the disappointment is still fresh is hard — and it's exactly what stops a bad day becoming a bad month.

title: Criticism, confrontation and letting it go
paras: Planning brings a steady supply of criticism, and the occasional confrontation. Much of the criticism isn't really personal, however personal it feels. The objector attacking your recommendation is defending their home; the member questioning you is doing their job; the client complaining about a delay is anxious about money. Hear these as comments on the situation, not judgements on your worth. There's a difference between caring about the quality of your advice and taking every disagreement as a personal blow.

Confrontation is handled best by staying calm. When someone's aggressive, pause before you answer rather than firing back, keep your voice level, and stick to the planning issues rather than personal ground. You can't control how the other person behaves, only whether you match it — and refusing to match it stops the exchange escalating. Afterwards, close it off: a word with a colleague, a short walk. Don't replay it at midnight — it'll look far smaller in the morning.

title: Leaving work at work
paras: Leaving work at work is one of the most important coping skills, and one of the hardest. Planning is absorbing, full of problems the mind chews over at all hours, and modern working only makes it worse — the laptop on the kitchen table, the phone carrying email into the evening. But the planner who never switches off isn't more dedicated. They're just denying themselves the recovery that keeps judgement sharp and enjoyment alive, heading towards being worn out.

Drawing the line takes effort, but the mechanics are simple. Decide when your working day ends, and most evenings keep to it. Resist the after-hours inbox — it rarely achieves anything except turning a quiet evening into a worried one, over something that could have waited. Find a ritual that marks the change from work to home: a walk, a change of clothes, shutting the study door. For many the commute did this, which is why home working blurs the line so badly. The report will still be there tomorrow, and you'll do it better rested. Protecting your own time isn't a lack of commitment — it's what makes a long one possible.

title: The unglamorous basics that actually work
paras: Some of the most effective ways of coping are so ordinary that professionals are almost embarrassed to take them seriously — and neglect them at their cost. Take your breaks: a short walk from the desk at lunchtime does more for the afternoon than a sandwich over the keyboard. Take your annual leave — all of it — in proper blocks, not odd days when you're already desperate. Leave taken before you're exhausted is worth twice as much as leave taken after, and the planners who wear their unused holiday as a badge are usually closest to running out of steam.

Body and mind aren't separate, and looking after one protects the other. Regular exercise — any kind you'll keep up — is one of the most reliable ways of managing pressure and clearing a cluttered head. Time outdoors does something no willpower at a desk can match. And sleep matters more than any of it — planners badly underrate it. Tired judgement is poor judgement, and the decisions and emails you regret are almost always made when you're exhausted. The planners who stay sharp for decades are, almost without exception, the ones who look after these unglamorous foundations.

title: Steadying yourself — attention and breathing
paras: Two simple techniques are worth spelling out plainly, because they're genuinely useful and too often wrapped in language that puts practical people off. The first is mindfulness, which sounds mystical and isn't. Strip away the mystique and it's training your attention: noticing when your mind has wandered off the task in front of you, and gently bringing it back. A short spell each day, sitting quietly and attending to your breathing, refocusing each time it wanders, makes a real difference to how settled and focused you feel. You need nothing more than a few quiet minutes, and the payoff is down to earth: better focus, less mental clutter, more distance from worry.

The second is even simpler, and works in the moment. Before a difficult meeting, a committee appearance or an awkward call, a few slow, deliberate breaths steady the nerves — in slowly, hold for a second, out slowly, a handful of times. This isn't a trick or a therapy — it's basic physiology, the same thing actors do in the wings, and it works because slow breathing calms the body's alarm response. Give yourself that moment, rather than rushing in flustered, and you'll speak more steadily and think more clearly.

title: A life outside planning
paras: Perhaps the deepest source of perspective is also the simplest: having a life that isn't about planning at all. The planner whose entire identity is bound up in the job has no shock absorber when it goes badly, because a bad week at work becomes a bad week at everything. The one who also has a family they enjoy, friends outside the profession, a sport or hobby that absorbs them comes to the difficult Monday with ballast. A refusal stings less when it's one part of a full life, not the whole of it.

This isn't an argument for caring less — the best planners care a great deal. It's an argument for not letting the job be the only thing you care about. Protect the time for the people and interests that matter to you as fiercely as you protect a deadline, and hold on to the friendships that will be there whatever this week's appeal decides. The planners who stay balanced are almost always the ones who were never only planners.

title: When you are no longer coping
paras: There are times when the pressure genuinely gets on top of someone — and the most important thing to say is this: recognising it and speaking up is a sign of good judgement, not of failure. Everyone, at every level, has periods of not coping well; it's a normal part of a long working life, not a weakness and nothing to be ashamed of. The signs are the ones we described — exhaustion that rest doesn't fix, lost enjoyment, sleep and temper going, that sense of being permanently overwhelmed. When they settle in and stay, the responsible response isn't to grit your teeth and push harder, which usually makes it worse — it's to talk to someone.

Who you talk to matters less than that you do. A trusted colleague, mentor or manager can help you put things in proportion, lighten a load, or remind you you're not the only one who's felt this way. And if it's persistent or serious, see a healthcare professional — your G-P is the natural first step, just as you would about a persistent physical problem. There's no medal for struggling on alone, and a lot to be said for dealing with something early, while it's small. Asking for help isn't the end of a good career — very often it's what protects one.

And if any of this is landing close to home, there's no threshold you have to reach before reaching out. Samaritans are free, day or night — call one one six, one two three. Shout is a crisis text line, open twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week — text eight five, two five eight. Your G-P is the natural first step for anything persistent. And the full support directory is in the Where to Turn topic of Under Pressure.

title: Key messages
paras: So, to finish — the key messages. One: pressure can't be eliminated, only managed, so stop waiting for it to go and get good at carrying it. Two: tell temporary pressure from chronic stress — short bursts are normal, even useful, but exhaustion a weekend can't fix, lost enjoyment and disrupted sleep over months are a signal to act. Three: keep a sense of proportion — after a setback, ask whether it'll matter in a year; usually not, and one decision isn't a verdict on your ability. Four: don't catastrophise; the mind runs to the worst and it's almost always lying.

Five: take criticism without absorbing it — most of it is about the situation, not you. Six: stay calm in confrontation, then set it down; pause before answering, keep your voice level, and don't replay it at midnight. Seven: leave work at work — decide when the day ends, resist the after-hours inbox, and mark the change from work to home. Eight: respect the unglamorous basics — breaks, all your annual leave in proper blocks, exercise, time outdoors, and sleep, because tired judgement is poor judgement.

Nine: use attention and breathing — a few quiet minutes a day, and a few slow breaths before committee, genuinely steady you. Ten: have a life outside planning; guard the time for family, friends and interests as fiercely as a deadline. Eleven: resilience is built, not born — everyone has periods of pressure, and steadiness develops over time. And twelve: speaking up is good judgement, not failure; when the signs settle in and stay, talk to a colleague, mentor or manager, and if it's persistent or serious, to your G-P.
